extra.message: Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY ('Keep it secret, keep it safe'). Flask signs its client-side session cookies (including the flask_login session that carries the authenticated user id) with this key. Anyone who knows the key from the source code can forge a valid session cookie and impersonate any user, including admin — a full authentication bypass.

Flask DEBUG mode is enabled (app.config['DEBUG'] = True). If the app is served with the Werkzeug development server, the interactive debugger is exposed, which can allow remote code execution via the debugger console, and detailed stack traces leak sensitive information.

Passwords are stored in cleartext: the User model keeps password as a plain String column, login compares it directly (app/blueprints/login/views.py:17 'user.password == password'), and change_password writes the new password unhashed (app/blueprints/account_area/views.py:35). No hashing (e.g. werkzeug.security.generate_password_hash) is used anywhere; a database leak exposes all user credentials immediately.

cwe: CWE-256: Plaintext Storage of a Password

extra.message: Missing authentication: MessagesView.post (POST /api/v1/messages/) has no @admin_required or @login_required decorator, unlike the sibling index/get/delete methods. Any unauthenticated attacker can create arbitrary Message records with attacker-controlled 'message' and 'from_user' fields, which are then rendered unescaped ('| safe') in the admin panel — the delivery vector for stored XSS against the admin.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: Missing CSRF protection: state-changing POST routes (change_password here, and change_email/send_feedback at lines 41/61) rely solely on the session cookie and use no CSRF token (no Flask-WTF or equivalent anywhere in the app). An attacker site can submit cross-origin form posts to change a logged-in victim's password or email. The same applies to /auth/logout and /auth/login which also accept GET requests.

The after_request handler explicitly sets 'X-XSS-Protection: 0' on every response whenever the per-session toggle is off (the default), actively disabling the browser's built-in XSS filter — a deliberate weakening of a security protection mechanism.

The 'name' cookie is set without HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite attributes. Because the cookie value is later rendered unescaped (XSS), the missing HttpOnly flag also leaves it fully readable/modifiable from JavaScript.

The add_admin management command defaults to creating the admin account with password 'admin' (def add_admin(password='admin')), and the login template (app/blueprints/login/templates/login/login.html:5) even advertises 'Use credentials "admin/admin"'. Deployments created with the default have a publicly documented, easily guessable admin credential; since is_admin is determined solely by username == 'admin' (app/models/models.py:21), this grants full administrative access.

Sensitive data exposure by design: the User.serialize property includes the plaintext 'password' field (line 27) and is returned by UsersView.index in app/blueprints/api/views.py:72. Note: UsersView is never registered (only MessagesView.register(api) at api/views.py:104), so this is currently unreachable via routes, but any future registration of UsersView would leak all user passwords over the API.

cwe: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
